newsitem.title: GERMANY: German region close to jobs deal in metal sector.
newsitem.headline: German region close to jobs deal in metal sector.

text.p: German trade union IG Metall and employers in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said on Thursday that they were near a deal on job protection measures demanded by the union as part of wider 1997 wage talks.

There are hopes that any deal reached by regional negotiators in the southwest state could then be used as a pilot agreement for a national solution to the pay dispute currently dogging Germany's metal and engineering sector.

IG Metall regional head Gerhard Zambelli told journalists during a break in negotiations that "important differences" between the two sides had now been resolved on so-called "employment security" measures.

"Agreement could be reached by the end of the day," Zambelli said. Dieter Hundt, chief negotiator for the Gesamtmetall engineering employers federation, agreed that the two were close to an agreement.

Some 3,000 workers from the region earlier demonstrated outside the talks venue against proposed cuts to sick pay entitlements, the issue at the heart at the current wave of protests that has hit German companies from Daimler-Benz to Siemens AG.
The two sides said the discussions, which are set to continue on Friday, had not yet touched on sick pay.

IG Metall last month said it wanted to channel over half of its 1997 pay demand to measures intended to protect and create employment in the industry, where sluggish domestic growth and foreign competition are costing over 100,000 jobs each month.
Reductions in the amount of overtime worked and a shorter working day have been suggested as possible ways of maintaining staff numbers in the industry.
But employers are unwilling to accept such measures unless it can secure cuts -- such as in sick pay, holiday and Christmas bonuses -- that mean overall labour costs do not rise in 1997.

Zambelli said that none of the measures discussed in the latest talks would imply an increase in labour costs for employers. IG Metall has said it will accept a 1997 pay rise in line with inflation if accompanied by concrete job guarantees.
The Baden-Wuerttemberg talks cover about 800,000 engineering workers, around a third of the total number employed in the metal and engineering sectors.
IG Metall has staged several days of protests involving temporary stoppages by hundreds of thousands of workers.
The workers demonstrated against planned cuts in pay to 80 percent during sickness, made possible by laws which came into force last month.
